It often circles over forest edge, or waits for long periods on a dead branch high in a tree. It uses thermals to circle and call, and is one of the commonest raptors of South China's hills. A resident.

features.v: A black crest on the crown with white tips, fanned when excited — apart from the name, the most conspicuous feature of the bird.
In flight the underwing is dark brown with a broad black subterminal band and dense white spotting, the tips black — a powerful contrast.
Upperparts dark brown, underparts pale brown finely barred, tail with a broad black subterminal band and a white tip.
Iris bright yellow, bare skin around the eye yellow, the stare formidable.

she-diao.summary: A black and white crest on the crown, and in flight a broad black band and dense white spotting beneath the wing — like a blackboard covered in writing. It really does eat snakes, venomous ones included.
she-diao.tagline: A hawk that lives on snakes, with a blackboard under each wing
she-diao.tip: A nationally protected species (Class II). Listen for that trembling whistle overhead, then look up for the circling hawk and check the underwing for the black band and the white spots.
she-diao.voice: A very loud whistle, 'kiiu—kiiu' or 'peee-uu', tremulous, often repeated while circling — the main way to find the bird.

shu-ma-que.behavior: Intensely sociable, feeding on the ground in hopping flocks of a dozen to a hundred and taking grain, grass seed, insects and human food scraps. Very alert: one bird flushes and the flock follows. Nests in wall cavities, roof tiles, air-conditioner holes and lamp housings, and will take over other birds' nest boxes. Dust-bathes enthusiastically on dry ground.

features.v: Chestnut crown, white cheeks, and a clear black ear-patch — that patch separates it from the House Sparrow.
Black from throat to upper breast like a small bib, in sharp contrast with the white cheeks.
Chestnut-brown back heavily streaked black; two white wingbars; buffy rump; dark brown tail.
Male and female look alike (unlike House Sparrow), so they are hard to tell apart in the field.

shu-ma-que.summary: The sparrow is too common to look at closely, which is why almost nobody does. Get near one and the design shows: a chestnut crown, snow-white cheeks and a small black bib. It is the most numerous bird in the cities of the Pearl River Delta, and the one that has worked out how to live with us.
shu-ma-que.tagline: The most overlooked — and most ubiquitous — of neighbours
shu-ma-que.tip: It is a protected species in China: catching or trading wild sparrows is illegal. Ordinary as it looks, it is load-bearing in the urban food web — the staple prey of hawks and shrikes.
shu-ma-que.voice: A thin, insistent 'cheep' — the baseline background noise of any southern Chinese city. The breeding song is slightly more structured but still a string of single notes.

si-guang-liang-niao.behavior: A highly gregarious, tree-loving starling, gathering in winter in flocks of tens to over a hundred to feed on berries, and dropping to the ground for fallen fruit and insects. A winter visitor here from October to March in farmland, orchards and city parks. Roosts communally in street trees or bamboo.

features.v: Head and neck pale grey-white with a silky sheen; upperparts grey; wings black with white patches; tail black.
Overall grey-brown, the head not pale, plumage plain — easily separated from the male.
Bill coral red with a darker tip; legs orange-red and bright.
Bare orange-yellow skin around the eye, often read as an eye-ring, conspicuous against the pale head.

si-guang-liang-niao.summary: The male's head looks dusted with silk: pale grey-white with a satin sheen, set off by a coral-red bill. The Red-billed Starling is endemic to China; in winter a flock will descend on a fruiting tree and strip it bare.
si-guang-liang-niao.tagline: White head, grey body, red bill and red legs — a starling of the south
si-guang-liang-niao.tip: Against Crested Myna and Black-collared Starling: the Red-billed Starling is the palest of the three, with a grey-white head and neck and a red bill.
si-guang-liang-niao.voice: Noisy: a harsh single 'jriii' or 'chreee', very loud when the whole flock calls, with softer whistles mixed in.

wu-dong.behavior: Usually turning over lawns and leaf litter for earthworms and insects, and eating berries. Strongly territorial when breeding, chasing birds larger than itself and even cats. The deep cup nest is reinforced with mud inside and hidden in a fork, on a wall or in a trellis. The city population is resident all year — one of the few songbirds that gives a concert in every season.

features.v: All black, orange-yellow bill, a ring of golden skin around the eye, dark brown legs. In sunlight the black takes on a fine blue-grey sheen.
Dark brown above, paler and finely streaked on the throat, bill duller and often brownish.
Brown with heavy spotting on the breast, very unlike the adult and often taken for another species.
Round and sturdy, fairly long-tailed; hops on the ground and stands upright when it stops.

wu-dong.summary: At first glance a black bird; look again and there is a golden eye-ring and an orange-yellow bill. The Chinese Blackbird is the tenor of southern cities: on a March morning it stands on a rooftop or a treetop and sings the whole street quiet.
wu-dong.tagline: A black suit, and the best voice in town
wu-dong.tip: A solo with real melody, complete phrases and a little improvisation is almost certainly a blackbird. The bird singing loudly at night in the city is usually this species too, confused by street lighting.
wu-dong.voice: A fluent, long, highly musical song, often ending with mimicry of other birds or even phone ringtones, delivered solo from a high perch at dawn and dusk. The call is a sharp 'chook-chook-chook' or a thin 'tseee', repeated when alarmed.

xiao-bai-yao-yu-yan.behavior: Almost never lands: it feeds, mates and even sleeps on the wing. Very fast, often circling buildings in groups of dozens. Nests in bridge arches, under high eaves and in rock crevices, using saliva mixed with feathers. A summer visitor here, common over the city from March to October.

features.v: Sooty black-brown all over, slightly paler at the throat, with a clear white band across the rump — the most visible feature in flight.
Long, narrow and scythe-shaped, held fully open like a bow — quite unlike the pointed wings of a swallow.
Short and shallowly forked, appearing square when spread.
Torpedo-shaped, small-headed and short-billed; the wings are more than twice the body length, built for speed.

xiao-bai-yao-yu-yan.summary: Swifts have such short legs that they can barely take off from the ground — so they spend almost their whole lives airborne. At dusk they scream between the tower blocks: a fixed item on the southern summer evening.
xiao-bai-yao-yu-yan.tagline: The flying fish that almost never lands
xiao-bai-yao-yu-yan.tip: Versus Barn Swallow: swifts have longer, more curved wings, an all-dark body, a white rump, fly higher and faster, and almost never perch on wires.
xiao-bai-yao-yu-yan.voice: A shrill 'sreee' or 'skreee', repeated and overlapping across a flock, high-pitched and penetrating.

xiao-pi-ti.behavior: Aquatic all its life and rarely out of the water. It dives for small fish, prawns and aquatic insects, each dive lasting 10–30 seconds. When alarmed it often sinks until only the head shows, or simply dives away. It nests on a floating platform in emergent vegetation that rises and falls with the water, and adults routinely carry chicks on their backs.

features.v: Head, neck and upper breast chestnut, a bright pale-yellow patch at the gape, yellow eye — warm-toned throughout.
Upperparts dark brown, underparts pale buff, sides of the neck whitish; plain, but the round body and tailless outline are unchanged.
Small and round, tail so short it is almost invisible, neck short, bill fine and pointed.
Legs set very far back, toes lobed — good for diving, hopeless for walking, so it hardly ever comes ashore.

xiao-pi-ti.summary: Round, short-tailed, floating like a fluffy little gourd. In breeding condition the cheeks and neck turn deep chestnut with a dab of yellow at the gape — that is its best look. When danger comes it says 'pff' and dives, surfacing several metres away.
xiao-pi-ti.tagline: A little gourd on the water — dive, and it is simply gone
xiao-pi-ti.tip: See a small brown ball with no tail on the water? Before you start looking for a duck, watch whether it dives. If it stays under for tens of seconds and comes up well away, it is a Little Grebe.
xiao-pi-ti.voice: In the breeding season a fast, tremulous trill, 'bibibi—bibibi', like a small ball bouncing on a table; also a single whistled 'bee'. A reliable clue that the bird is present.

ye-lu.behavior: Active from dusk through the night. By day it roosts in flocks in trees, often nesting alongside Little Egrets and pond herons. It takes fish, prawns, frogs and aquatic insects, and will also take the chicks of other birds. Extremely common along city rivers and around park lakes, and highly tolerant of man-made surroundings. In flight the neck is drawn in and the feet barely project, giving a compact, thickset silhouette.

features.v: Crown, nape and back black with a green-blue gloss; two or three long thin white plumes trail from the nape.
Wings and rump grey, cleanly divided from the black back — perched, it looks as though it has thrown a grey shawl over its shoulders.
Chin, throat, breast and belly white to pale grey, sharply contrasting.
Iris brilliant red in adults, bill black and heavy; legs yellow-green.

ye-lu.summary: By day it tucks its head into its shoulders and squats in a tree like a grey-black ball, easy to overlook. At dusk those red eyes light up and it finally goes to work — the night heron, as the name says, is the heron on night duty.
ye-lu.tagline: Red eyes and white braids — the heron that works the night shift
ye-lu.tip: Wait by a park lake at dusk: as the light goes, a few 'grey balls' lift out of the trees, each croaking once as it rises — that is the night shift heading out.
ye-lu.voice: On night flights often a hoarse 'quark' or 'wok', short and frog-like — the easiest sound to place after dark. Noisy at the colony, with a range of mutterings.

zao-juan.behavior: A brood parasite: the female lays in the nests of Black-collared Starlings, Crested Mynas and crows, which raise the chick. Feeds mainly on fruit, especially figs, often in flocks in a fruiting tree. Secretive, staying high in the canopy and singing with the bill open and the head thrown back.

features.v: All black with blue-green metallic gloss in sunlight; eye bright red; bill pale greenish grey; long tail.
Brown above, densely spotted and barred white; white below with bold dark barring — so different from the male that it is often taken for another species.
Crow-sized, with a long broad tail; in flight the outline is that of a small crow.
Bill stout and slightly downcurved; the male's red eye is conspicuous in shade.

zao-juan.summary: You may never have seen it, but you have certainly heard it. From March to August, at five in the morning across the Delta, a two-note whistle rising and quickening — that is the Koel declaring summer. It hides in dense canopy and almost never shows itself.
zao-juan.tagline: The bird that starts the southern summer
zao-juan.tip: The rising two-note whistle is the identification. To see one, follow the sound up into a tall canopy and look for a black silhouette; the male's red eye catches the light against the sky.
zao-juan.voice: A two-note 'ko-el', the first short and low, the second higher and longer, repeated dozens of times and accelerating — pitch and pace rising until it sounds frantic. Loudest at dawn and dusk, and often at night under street lights, which makes it a well-known cause of lost sleep in Zhuhai.

zhong-bai-lu.behavior: Stands or walks slowly at the edge of shallow water, fish ponds and flats, taking fish, shrimp, frogs and aquatic insects. Usually alone or in small groups, mixing with Little and Great Egrets in winter. A winter visitor here from October to April at all kinds of wetland.

features.v: Yellow, black in the breeding season, often with a dark tip; medium length — shorter than Great Egret's, longer and finer than Little's.
The gape line ends below the eye or just past its rear edge and does not extend conspicuously beyond the eye — the most reliable separation from Great Egret.
Legs black; feet yellow to black — between Little Egret (yellow feet) and Great Egret (all black).
About 65 cm long; neck long but less extreme than Great Egret's; stands fairly upright.

zhong-bai-lu.summary: Between Little and Great Egret in size, with a yellow bill, black legs and yellow feet — nothing extreme, which is exactly why it is hard. One rule: if the gape stops short of the eye it is Intermediate; if it passes the eye it is Great.
zhong-bai-lu.tagline: The hardest of the three white egrets
zhong-bai-lu.tip: Three egrets, fast: all-black bill with yellow feet is Little; a yellow bill with the gape stopping short of the eye is Intermediate; a yellow bill, gape past the eye and black legs is Great.
zhong-bai-lu.voice: A hoarse 'kraak', similar to Little Egret but slightly lower, given repeatedly when flushed.

zhu-jing-ban-jiu.behavior: Feeds mostly by walking on the ground, taking grass seed, fallen fruit and human food debris; flushes almost vertically when startled. Usually in pairs or small parties, tolerant and thoroughly adapted to dense city. The nest is perfunctory — a platform of a few twigs — and it will lay on air-conditioner units, windowsills and flower pots, which is why it so often ends up living in the same building as we do.

features.v: A broad black patch from the sides of the neck to the nape, densely spotted white — the single most reliable mark.
Head grey-brown; back and wings pinkish brown with pale fringes giving a scaly look; underparts pale pink-buff; long tail with large white tips to the outer feathers.
Plump, small-headed and long-tailed; bill slender and short with a soft base; legs purplish red.
Loud wing-claps on take-off and landing, a bounding flight, and conspicuous white tail tips when the tail is fanned.

zhu-jing-ban-jiu.summary: Often mistaken for a pigeon, but the black collar scattered with white dots settles it at once. The Spotted Dove walks with a nodding head and clatters loudly into flight — the most everyday sound of any housing estate in the Pearl River Delta.
zhu-jing-ban-jiu.tagline: A 'wild pigeon' wearing a collar of pearls
zhu-jing-ban-jiu.tip: Don't call it a pigeon too quickly: feral pigeons are stockier and have unspotted necks. A pearl collar means Spotted Dove.
zhu-jing-ban-jiu.voice: A three-note 'coo-coo-coo', the last note drawn out and falling, repeated for long stretches — one of the most soporific sounds of a southern afternoon. Courting males add a low rolling growl while bowing and spreading the tail.

zong-bei-bo-lao.behavior: A classic sit-and-wait hunter: perches on a high dead twig, wire or reed tip, drops fast onto prey and returns to the same place to eat it. Strongly territorial when breeding, chasing birds much larger than itself. Caches food by impaling prey on thorns or barbed wire. Lives in open scrub and farmland and is the commonest shrike at low altitude.

features.v: Crown grey to black with a broad black band through the eye; that glare is the classic shrike look.
Back and scapulars rufous (varying between subspecies); wings black with white patches; throat white; breast and belly pale buff, flanks washed orange.
Black and stout, with a clear hook and tooth at the tip of the upper mandible, used to sever a victim's neck.
Very long — nearly half the total length — and frequently swung side to side or in circles, a useful mark when perched.

zong-bei-bo-lao.summary: Twenty-odd centimetres long with the heart of a raptor: black mask, hooked bill, hard stare. The Long-tailed Shrike takes insects, lizards, mice and even small birds, and impales what it cannot finish on thorns to dry — its most famous habit.
zong-bei-bo-lao.tagline: An eagle's eye on a sparrow's body — the little butcher
zong-bei-bo-lao.tip: A long-tailed bird with a black mask on a paddy-bund wire or a dead twig is almost certainly this species. If you find insects or small lizards hanging on thorns, you have found its larder.
zong-bei-bo-lao.voice: Harsh and grating, like a rusty hinge: 'zha-zha-zha' or 'ge-ge', dry in tone. It also mimics other birds — sometimes better than the original — which is how it draws small birds close enough to catch.

zong-shan-wei-ying.behavior: Lives in tall grass, paddies and marsh edges, skulking low in the vegetation. In the breeding season the male sings on a bounding display flight to claim territory. Eats insects and grass seed. Present all year here, but sings hardest in spring and autumn.

features.v: Brown above with heavy black streaking on the back; pale supercilium; underparts pale buff with a whiter throat.
Short and broad with clear white tips, fanned like a little fan — hence the name.
Crown brown and finely streaked; bill short and thick, blunter than Plain Prinia's.
The display flight is a pronounced series of bounds, each rise accompanied by a call — the easiest way to confirm the species in the field.

zong-shan-wei-ying.summary: It has an unmistakable flight: bouncing through the air in steps, calling once per bounce, so the trajectory reads as a dotted line. Land, and it disappears into the grass for good.
zong-shan-wei-ying.tagline: Calls 'zit' with every bounce, like a wound-up toy
zong-shan-wei-ying.tip: A small bird moving through the air in bounces, one call per bounce, can be identified on the spot — none of the other common warblers here fly like that.
zong-shan-wei-ying.voice: A single 'zit' or 'zitting', short and nasal, given every second or two in flight with metronomic regularity — like a sewing machine, or something being wound up.
